libxml2.reason: Observed offline with native libxml2 2.9.13 on unchanged explicit roots and file bytes: schema assessed invalid. Source-qualified interpretation I-012 retains XSD 1.0 anySimpleType constructor acceptance. Literal absent-variety rules support exclusion; W3C stE053 explicitly expects its union valid in 1.0 and invalid in 1.1. List acceptance has weaker historical support. The stricter 1.1 rule is not treated as a published 1.0 amendment, so this split is not classified as a confirmed processor defect. All 1 declared instances are blocked by schema rejection; no instance validity is inferred.

Instance validity follows the derived a particle bounds, so zero, one, two and four a children are valid. Base-only b and unknown c are independently invalid. Base first permits Choice[0,unbounded](a[0,unbounded],b), so the derived a mapping has independently matching member bounds. The non-singleton optional tail choice preserves a DFA consumer while source restriction and ordinary shared-group consumers reference the same Restricted group. Two a children with no tail, c or d are valid; b, two tail alternatives and a after the tail violate explicit derived particles. The Base declaration accepts b, while legal xsi:type=Derived selects the same restricted content and rejects b without capping repeated a. All named leaves have explicit xs:string types.

Closed ordinary controls distinguish removal of unsupported execution metadata from weakening particle semantics. Required a[1,unbounded] restricts RequiredBase Choice[0,unbounded](a[1,unbounded],b): both member ranges match and the synthetic outer unit fits, so empty is invalid and one, two or four a children are valid. FiniteDerived a[2,3] structurally restricts base Choice[0,unbounded](a[0,3],b): the synthetic outer unit range fits, and 2..3 narrows the matching a branch 0..3. It accepts exactly two or three a children and rejects zero, one or four. DirectChoice has a unit outer choice, so one branch is chosen: its a[0,unbounded] branch admits empty and repeated a; its b[1,1] branch admits one b, while mixed a/b and repeated b remain invalid. Removing a derived cap cannot flatten these independent bounds or erase the choice partition.
